sources.quote: Nadrian (Ned) C. Seeman (1945–2021, Figs. 1 and 2) was born in Chicago.
While being a medical undergraduate at the University of Chicago, he realized that research could also be a profession and decided to pursue such a career.
followed by postdoctoral work first at Columbia University
and, then, with the legendary crystallographer, Alexander Rich, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
and, then, with the legendary crystallographer, Alexander Rich, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
In 1977, Seeman was appointed to the Biology Department of the State University of New York at Albany.
By then, he had already become a member of the Faculty of the Department of Chemistry of New York University where he stayed to the end of his life.

note: Developed life motif constructing three-dimensional DNA structures based on Holliday junction concept.

sources.quote: Playing with its model led Seeman to develop his life motif, constructing three-dimensional DNA structures, and he became a nano-architect.
And, to top it all, he was co-recipient of the Kavli Prize in Nanoscience in 2010, shared with another pioneer of the field, Donald Eigler of IBM Almaden Research Center in San Jose, CA.

note: Shared Kavli Prize in Nanoscience in 2010.

sources.quote: shared with another pioneer of the field, Donald Eigler of IBM Almaden Research Center in San Jose, CA.
Among his many research papers, he published a beautiful article, one of the first features in the fledgling magazine of the culture of chemistry, The Chemical Intelligencer [1].
One of his last publications appeared in 2020 in which he looked back at 40 years of DNA nanotechnology [2].
